references.text: In Matthew 12:10-12, the Pharisees ask Jesus whether it is lawful to heal on the Sabbath, and Jesus answers that it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath—the same theme found in Luke 6:9.
Mark 3:4 is the parallel passage to Luke 6:9 where Jesus asks the same question in the synagogue: "Is it lawful to do good or to do evil on the Sabbath, to save life or to kill?"
In Luke 14:3, Jesus again asks the Pharisees whether it is lawful to heal on the Sabbath, showing that this was a recurring point of contention.

The synagogue ruler reacts with anger because Jesus healed on the Sabbath, but Jesus defends himself by pointing out that people untie their ox or donkey even on the Sabbath—relevant to the question of doing good on the Sabbath.
In John 7:23, Jesus argues that if circumcision is performed on the Sabbath to uphold the Law of Moses, one should not be angry that he makes an entire person well on the Sabbath.
Matthew 12:1-8 provides the context for the Sabbath controversy where Jesus declares himself Lord of the Sabbath, which underlies his authoritative question in Luke 6:9.
Jesus says that the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath, and that the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath—this supports his argument that it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath.
Deuteronomy 23:25 shows that the law allowed picking grain from another's field, which is relevant to the broader Sabbath controversy surrounding Luke 6:9.
Hosea 6:6 says "I desire mercy, not sacrifice"—a principle Jesus quotes in Matthew 12:7 during the parallel Sabbath discussion to justify that doing good takes precedence.
Isaiah 58:13-14 speaks of keeping the Sabbath holy and making it a day of joy for the Lord, which provides background for the question of what is right to do on the Sabbath.
